L7@P0: Abstract
L8@P0: Bulgarian Solitaire, originally a recreational mathematics topic about pile sizes of
L9@P0: various objects under a rearrangement procedure, is now studied as an operation
L10@P0: on the integer partitions of a fixed number. Martin Gardner popularized the mathematical puzzle in one of his late Scientific American columns, but the unusual
L11@P0: name comes from an earlier article by Henrik Eriksson in the Swedish language
L12@P0: journal Elementa. That article ends with a variant game which does not yet seem
L13@P0: to have been fully analyzed. Here we provide a thorough study of Henrik Eriksson’s
L14@P0: Bulgarian Solitaire variant and its immediate generalizations, also placing these in
L15@P0: the context of several broad generalizations of Bulgarian Solitaire developed in the
L16@P0: past ten years. Of particular interest, characterizing and enumerating the Garden of
L17@P0: Eden states (those with no predecessors under the operation) uses a new “stretched”
L18@P0: version of Dyson’s rank statistic for integer partitions.
L19@P0: – In memory of Henrik Eriksson (1942–2017)

L16: ## Abstract
L17: Suppose k students sit in a circle and are each distributed some initial amount of candy. Each student begins with an even amount of candy, but their individual amounts may vary. Upon the teacher’s signal, each student passes half of their candy to their left and keeps half. After this step, any student with an odd amount of candy receives an extra piece. The game ends if all the students are holding the same amount of candy.
L18: We prove, in a generalized setting, that for any initial distribution of n pieces of candy, the game terminates after O(log n) many iterations and each student ends with ^{n}_{k} +O(log n) many pieces. Moreover, there exist initial distributions for which the O(log n) term cannot be improved.

L132: $p_{N,K;A,B,C}$ ... pop-stacked permutations of $[N]$ with $K$ runs; last run of shape $(A...BC)$. \[\begin{aligned} p_{N,K;A,B,C} = {} & [A = B = C] \sum_{a=1}^{A-1} \sum_{b=1}^{N-1} \sum_{c=A}^{N-1} p_{N-1,K-1;a,b,c} \\ & + [A = B < C] \sum_{a=1}^{C-2} \sum_{b=1}^{N-2} \sum_{c=A}^{N-2} p_{N-2,K-1;a,b,c} \\ & + [A < B < C] \sum_{b = A}^{B-1} p_{N-1, K; A, b, C-1} \end{aligned}\]

L7: cite3†pdf | cite4†pdf L8: ### Candy Sharing Game Rules
L9:   * The players should sit in a circle.
L10:   * Each circle will have a leader who starts the game by distributing wrapped candies among participants. The distribution of candy will not necessarily be even -- some playerswill start out with more and some players may start out with none.
L11:   * During the game, players should keep their candy on the ground in front of them. They should make sure that the candy does not get lost under their legs and they should not hold it in their hands.
L12:   * When the leader says ``Share!'', everyone who has two or more pieces of candy in front of them gives one piece to the person on their right and one piece to the person on their left. They should use both arms to do this at the same time. Players with one or zero pieces of candy do nothing.
L13:   * After the appropriate players have shared candy, the leader will say ``Share!'' again. This process repeats until the group sees a pattern emerge in the game.
L14:   * Several things might happen with the game.
L15:     1. The game might stop because no one is passing candy any more.
L16:     2. The game might settle down so that even though everyone passes candy every time, the amount of candy that each player has is always the same. This is called a fixed point.
L17:     3. A repeating pattern might emerge in the way that the candy is shared. This is called a cycle.
L18: ### Candy Sharing Game Challenges
L19:   * Find an initial distribution of candy that eventually causes the game to stop. That is, tell the leader how to arrange the candy so that some players pass candy a few times, but then all players stop passing candy. What distribution or distribution strategy did you use to do this?
L20:   * Find an initial distribution of candy that leads to a fixed point. Remember that a fixed point happens when everyone passes candy, but the amount of candy in front of each person stays the same after each pass. What distribution or distribution strategy did you use?
L21:   * Find an initial distribution of candy that leads to a cycle. A cycle happens when there is a repeating pattern of sharing that never stops. What distribution or distribution strategy did you use?
L22: Consider the following questions as a group and experiment to figure them out.
L23:   * What is the smallest amount of candy that you can use to design a game that never stops?
L24:   * What is the smallest amount of candy that you can use if you want to guarantee that the game will never stop no matter how the leader distributes the candy? (This question is slightly different from the previous question because in that question you were allowed to tell the leader how to distribute the candy.)
L25:   * What is the largest amount of candy that you can use if you want a game that leads to a cycle instead of a fixed point?
L26:   * What is the smallest amount of candy that you can use if you want to design a game that leads to a fixed point?
L27:   * What is the smallest amount of candy that you can use if you want to guarantee that the game will lead to a fixed point no matter how the leader distributes the candy?
L28: ### Changing The Rules
L29: 
L30: After you have tried the challenges on the next page, you might want to try changing the rules of the game. For example, you might try a version where the players always pass half their candy to the person on their left (keeping one more than they pass if they have an odd number). What kinds of eventual patterns emerge in this game?
